description:
We are building a passionate and innovative team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our aim is to bring together talented individuals with diverse skills and ideas to collaborate, solve real-world challenges, and create innovative solutions using science and technology.

We are looking for team members interested in programming, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, data science, web development, UI/UX design, astronomy, space science, electronics, and research
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational platform designed to give young students a virtual experience of space exploration. It allows users to take part in simulated astronaut missions, manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food and power, and make important decisions to complete missions successfully while keeping the crew safe.

The project addresses the challenge by turning the complex concepts of space missions into an engaging and easy-to-understand learning experience. Through interactive scenarios and mission-based activities, students can explore the responsibilities and difficulties astronauts face in space.

Our goal is to make space education more interesting and accessible, encourage critical thinking and problem-solving, and inspire young learners to develop an interest in science, technology and future space exploration.
details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive web simulator where students run a space outpost as a junior astronaut or a mission commander. Its goal is to make astronaut training hands-on instead of textbook-based.

What it does and how it works: Students choose a Moon or Mars mission and manage the outpost's power, oxygen, water and food. They monitor crew health and respond to unexpected emergencies. Each session ends with a score and an evaluation. The platform has seven connected systems: Life Support, Power Management, Radiation Protection, Food Production, Mission Control, Emergency Simulation and a Scoring System. Because the systems affect each other, students see the trade-offs of a real mission. For example, using power to split water makes oxygen but leaves less water to drink.

Benefits and intended impact: Students rarely get to face the decisions astronauts make, and space engineering is hard to learn from theory alone. Our trainer builds understanding of Moon and Mars exploration, interest in STEM, resource management, problem-solving under pressure and systems thinking. It also shows what it takes to keep a crew alive far from Earth.

Tools and technologies: The app is built with React 18 and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind CSS in a dark aerospace design, with Three.js for 3D scenes and Zustand for state. Python is used for optional offline scientific calculations. It is live at https://astra-x-blue.vercel.app

Creativity: Instead of explaining space science, we turn it into a mission. Students choose a role and handle live telemetry and emergencies. The Moon and Mars have different gravity, day length, sunlight and radiation, so each destination plays differently.

Factors we considered: Scientific accuracy came first, so the simulation uses real NASA values such as 0.84 kg of oxygen per astronaut per day, 98% water recovery on the ISS, and solar and radiation figures for the Moon and Mars. We also considered learning value, ease of use for students, and public access through a web link. We tested mission scenarios and emergencies and fixed edge cases along the way.
